newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan minister says Friday strike unlawful.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan minister says Friday strike unlawful.

text.p: Kenya's labour minister declared unlawful on Thursday a national strike called for Friday by an alliance pressing for constitutional reforms and urged police to ensure it was a normal working day.

"The strike is going to be unlawful and it is an offence to participate in such activities, just as it is unlawful for anyone to incite workers to go out on strike," Labour Minister Philip Masinde told a news conference in the capital Nairobi.

"I would like to advise as well as appeal to the workers all over the country not to take the law into their own hands, to ignore the strike call and continue to do their work on the day mentioned," Masinde said.

"I urged the security (police) to take all measures to ensure the day passes as normal, to stop any activities that may be termed illegal," Masinde said, adding that once he declared the strike illegal police were bound to enforce the law.

The National Convention Executive Council (NCEC) called the general strike for Friday to press President Daniel arap Moi to implement constitutional reforms before elections. No date has been set for the polls.
Masinde's statement appeared to set the stage for clashes on Friday between NCEC supporters and riot police as the strike organisers have called for marches in support of the stoppage.

At least nine people were killed on July 7 during clashes between police and pro-reform demonstrators in Nairobi and other centres. The worst political violence in seven years rattled investors and tourists.
The NCEC has campaigned since May for reforms through rallies and demonstrations the government says are illegal.

Moi's government has offered a set of "minimal" changes before the elections and a full constitutional review after the elections but the NCEC argues that it was not consulted over what was offered and sees the measures as too little, too late.

Masinde said political parties and the NCEC were not legally authorised to call strikes and Friday's action appeared aimed at sabotaging the economy by stopping production that could not be recovered.
He said the NCEC consisted of "self-appointed individuals who do not speak on behalf of anyone".
The NCEC says it has a popular mandate to press for political and constitutional reforms to cut the power of Moi, 73 and ruler for 19 years.
"It is obvious that it (strike) will put the workers in trouble with their employers with the likely consequences of being dismissed from their jobs," Masinde added.
Masinde said the government could not discount incidents of violence breaking out on Friday as a few people were bent on breaking the law. He added that police would be vigilant.
Kenya's stock and foreign exchange markets have been shaken this week by the International Monetary Fund deciding last Thursday to cancel a key aid package in a row over corruption.
